The Indo-Pacific sergeant (Abudefduf vaigiensis) is a common damselfish found on coral reefs throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Field studies indicate that newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs after a brief incubation period, with the yolk-sac larva typically hatching following approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This relatively rapid embryonic development is characteristic of many pomacentrids and is linked to the warm, stable thermal conditions of tropical reef environments. Following hatching, the pelagic larva enters a planktonic phase that can last for several weeks, during which the larva relies on its endogenous yolk reserves before commencing first exogenous feeding upon mouth opening. The initial mass of the newly emerged prolarva is exceedingly small, with a wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0017 grams [Wwb = 0.0017 grams], a value derived from the oocyte dimensions typical of this genus; this minuscule size underscores the vulnerability of the earliest life stages to starvation and predation in the plankton.

As the pelagic teleost larva grows and develops, it undergoes substantial morphological transformation before reaching the reef-settlement stage. The juvenile recruits that eventually settle into benthic habitats are still far from their ultimate size, and growth proceeds steadily through the post-settlement juvenile phase. Based on asymptotic growth models fitted to length-at-age data from field-collected specimens, the ultimate total length attained by adult Abudefduf vaigiensis reaches approximately 20 centimeters [Li = approximately 20 centimeters]. This maximum recorded body length is consistent with values reported for other members of the genus, which typically range between 15 and 25 cm as adults. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length is calculated to be 242 grams [Wwi = 242 grams], reflecting the robust, laterally compressed body plan that characterizes sergeant majors. The relationship between length and mass follows a typical allometric scaling pattern for reef fishes, with the exponent approximating 3.07, indicating slightly positive allometric mass gain relative to length.

The onset of reproductive maturity in the Indo-Pacific sergeant is closely tied to body size rather than strictly to age, although both factors are correlated under natural conditions. Sexual maturation, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis and gonadal recrudescence, is estimated to occur when individuals reach a total length of approximately 12.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12.6 centimeters]. This total length at puberty represents a size threshold at which energy reserves become sufficient to support the metabolic demands of vitellogenesis and spermiation. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for a fish of this length is 58.6 grams [Wwp = 58.6 grams], a value derived from the same length-weight relationship used to estimate ultimate mass. Reaching this size typically requires several months to a year of post-settlement growth, depending on local food availability and competitive interactions. Congeneric species such as Abudefduf saxatilis show similar size thresholds for maturity, suggesting a conserved evolutionary pattern within the genus.

The maximum recorded longevity of Abudefduf vaigiensis in the wild, based on mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation, is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under the thermal conditions typical of its tropical reef habitat at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This life span is modest compared to some larger reef fishes but is comparable to that of other small-to-medium-bodied damselfishes, many of which live between 3 and 7 years. The relatively short maximum lifespan is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in which individuals invest in multiple reproductive bouts over several breeding seasons. Spawning activity in this species is strongly tied to the lunar cycle, with peak reproductive events often coinciding with the new and full moons. Gravid females produce multiple clutches during the protracted breeding season, and each spawning event yields a batch of demersal, adhesive eggs that are deposited on a hard substrate and aggressively guarded by the male until hatching.

Ecologically, the Indo-Pacific sergeant plays an important role in the reef community as both a planktivore and a substrate-competitor. Adults are typically observed in aggregations above the reef matrix, where they feed on zooplankton and benthic algae, and their nesting activities can have significant local impacts on the benthic community composition. The egg clutches, each containing several hundred eggs, are laid in a single layer and are subject to intense paternal care, including active fanning and defense against egg predators such as wrasses and other damselfishes. Under optimal temperature regimes, the incubation period lasting approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] ensures that embryonic development proceeds rapidly — a duration near the minimum for the genus and shorter than that documented in some temperate pomacentrids, reflecting the energetic advantages of warm-water spawning grounds where metabolic rates are elevated and yolk reserves are consumed more quickly. This rapid development minimizes the window of vulnerability to benthic predators and is a key adaptation to the high-predation environment of tropical coral reefs.
